title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
statement: Decide whether the integer array `nums` has three positions `i < j < k`, not necessarily next to each other, whose values strictly grow in that order: `nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]`. Return `true` if such positions exist and `false` if they do not.
notes:
## Intuition

The brute force tries every middle position and looks for a smaller value somewhere before it and a larger one somewhere after it, which costs O(n²). A single greedy pass is enough instead. Keep two numbers: `first`, the smallest value seen so far, and `second`, the smallest value seen so far that has something smaller before it. Keeping both as small as possible leaves the most room for a later value to beat them. As soon as a value is larger than `second`, a triplet exists.

## Approach

1. Start with `first = second = Infinity`.
2. For each `num`: if `num <= first`, it becomes the new `first`.
3. Otherwise, if `num <= second`, it becomes the new `second` (it has `first` before it and is bigger than it).
4. Otherwise `num` is bigger than `second`, which is itself bigger than some earlier value, so return `true`.
5. If the loop ends, no value ever passed `second`; return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. `1` is at most `Infinity`, so `first = 1`. `2` is bigger than `first` but at most `Infinity`, so `second = 2`. `3` is bigger than both, so the function returns `true` (the triplet `1, 2, 3`).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant work per value.
- Space: O(1): only `first` and `second`.

## Pitfalls

- Use `<=`, not `<`: equal values are not an increase, so `[1, 1, 1]` must stay `false`.
- Updating `first` after `second` is set looks wrong, since the new `first` comes after `second`. It is still safe: `second` keeps meaning "some value with a smaller one before it", and that smaller value still exists. In `[20, 100, 10, 12, 5, 13]` the pass ends with `first = 5`, `second = 12` and finds `13`; the real triplet is `10, 12, 13`.
- In Java or C, starting at `Integer.MAX_VALUE` / `INT_MAX` works only because of `<=`: a value equal to the maximum is stored, never mistaken for a third element.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `first` | smallest value seen so far |
| `second` | smallest value seen so far that has a smaller value before it |
| `num` | the current value |

narration.2: No value has been seen yet, so the smallest is Infinity.
narration.3: No value with a smaller one before it has been seen yet either.
narration.5: Look at the values from left to right.
narration.6: Not bigger than the smallest so far: it becomes the new smallest.
narration.7: Keeping first as low as possible makes a later second easier to find.
narration.8: Bigger than first but not bigger than second: it is a lower second.
narration.9: Remember it as the smallest value that has something smaller before it.
narration.11: Bigger than second, which has a smaller value before it: three increasing values exist.
narration.14: No value ever beat second, so there is no increasing triplet.
